differences.title: 1. DELIVERY MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Amazon SQS delivers messages to one consumer group: multiple pollers compete, and only one receives each message. Downstream parallelism scales horizontally without duplicating work across independent services by default.
differences.rightDesc: Google Cloud Pub/Sub is topic-based broadcast. Messages published to a topic can be delivered to many independent subscriptions, enabling true fan-out. Each subscription tracks its own offsets and acknowledgement state separately.

differences.title: 2. ACK / RETRY MECHANICS
differences.leftDesc: SQS uses a visibility timeout: after receive, the message becomes hidden for a period. If processing fails or the receiver doesn’t delete it, the message reappears for redelivery, supporting at-least-once delivery.
differences.rightDesc: Pub/Sub tracks acknowledgements per subscription. If a subscriber doesn’t ack before the ack deadline expires, Pub/Sub redelivers based on subscription policy. This decouples processing time from publisher throughput.

differences.title: 3. ORDERING GUARANTEES
differences.leftDesc: SQS ordering is limited: standard queues are effectively unordered, while FIFO queues provide ordering per message group using deduplication and group IDs. Throughput can constrain ordering under high concurrency.
differences.rightDesc: Pub/Sub provides ordering via message ordering keys. Messages with the same key are delivered in order to each subscription, but ordering is not guaranteed across different keys or different subscriptions, requiring careful key design.

differences.title: 4. MESSAGE DEDUPLICATION
differences.leftDesc: FIFO SQS can enable content-based or explicit deduplication IDs. The service suppresses duplicate messages within the deduplication interval, reducing accidental replays caused by producer retries.
differences.rightDesc: Pub/Sub does not universally provide FIFO deduplication. To achieve idempotency, producers/consumers typically use message IDs and store processing state (or implement dedupe in the consumer), especially under at-least-once semantics.

differences.title: 5. SCALING & THROUGHPUT CONTROLS
differences.leftDesc: SQS scales by increasing consumer pollers. You tune batch size and visibility timeout, and rely on backoff plus concurrent receives. Delivery is demand-driven: messages only leave the queue when polled.
differences.rightDesc: Pub/Sub supports push delivery (HTTP) or pull streaming with flow control. Subscribers can regulate in-flight messages via client settings, while Pub/Sub continuously streams data to available capacity, smoothing bursts.

differences.title: 6. RETENTION & DEAD-LETTERING
differences.leftDesc: SQS uses configurable retention periods and dead-letter queues (DLQs). After the max receive count is reached, messages are moved to the DLQ, enabling isolation of poison messages and safer retries.
differences.rightDesc: Pub/Sub offers message retention and dead-letter topics via subscription configuration. Unacknowledged or negatively processed messages can be routed after delivery attempts, keeping primary subscriptions clean while preserving traceability.

differences.title: 7. POSITION TRACKING & REPLAY
differences.leftDesc: SQS doesn’t maintain consumer offsets; once a message is received, it’s tracked via visibility and deletions. Replay typically happens by re-enqueuing or relying on redelivery, which complicates deterministic consumer recovery.
differences.rightDesc: Pub/Sub maintains per-subscription acknowledgement state and supports replay by resetting subscription seek/offsets or using retained subscriptions. This enables controlled reprocessing for new consumers and schema migrations.
